name: Timbe
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible
sweep_summary: Timbe (timb1251) is not in the catalog. The single stress-title hit, Talić 2018 (NLLT), is a Glottolog mis-tag: its lingbuzz abstract and the Springer page show it concerns accent shift to proclitics in a Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian dialect and never mentions Timbe or PNG (Glottolog's Timbe bibliography is polluted with unrelated 'Upward..' titles). Beyond the listed item, I recovered the dead-linked Foster 1981 'Timbe Grammar Sketch' from the the Internet Archive (124 pp., image-only; saved and front matter scanned): it is a discourse-cohesion study with no phonology section and no stress statement. Suter's open 2018 Cologne thesis on Huon Peninsula comparative morphology was downloaded and read; it has only reconstructive remarks (suffixes unstressed; presumed proto word accent on the verb-root initial syllable) and no Timbe word-stress statement, but its bibliography names the one phonological description, Foster & Foster 1972 'Timbe phonemics' (SIL Ukarumpa ms.), which is not online (SIL sites an automated-access block-403, OLAC/sealang could not be reached by automated download) — highest acquisition priority. McElhanon 1967 (Oceanic Linguistics) is JSTOR-only, medium priority. No first-hand statement of Timbe word-stress placement was read; no new stress statement was found. this compilation's was already exhausted, so all look-ups were direct downloads.

sources.citation: Suter, Edgar (2018). Comparative Morphology of the Huon Peninsula Languages (Papua New Guinea). PhD thesis, University of Cologne. viii+331 pp. (Glottolog ref 577703)
sources.quote: The *u I reconstruct was not lowered in Borong, Somba, Kinalaknga and Kumukio, presumably because the suffix *-utup carried no primary stress. The majority of the reflexes point to *u as the vowel of the second syllable, too, and this vowel also failed to be lowered in Borong, Somba and Timbe. [...] The reason for the many irregular phonological developments in the nominal number suffixes is probably the fact that they are unstressed.
sources.locator: extracted text(Western Huon plural suffix, p. ~130); lines 7363-7368 (habitual suffix); no Timbe-specific stress passage
sources.note: Only incidental, reconstructive remarks: suffixes presumed unstressed; a presumed 'unitary word accent on the first syllable of the verb root' in Proto-Huon habitual forms. No synchronic statement of where Timbe word stress falls. Its bibliography is the best pointer to the unobtained Foster & Foster 1972 'Timbe phonemics'.

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. (1984). A linguistic field guide to the Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-57.
sources.note: Nothing on phonology. Gives Timbe dialects (Central, North, South, North-divergent), village list, population 11,279, and the SIL team (Mr Michael and Mrs Margaret Foster, Kurung village, Central dialect).

sources.citation: McElhanon, K. A. (1975). North-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study 1, Pacific Linguistics C-38, pp. 527-567.
sources.note: Phonology section 2.8.1.4.1 (pp. 544-546) tabulates phonemes and syllable structure for ten representative languages (Kate, Ono, Selepet, Kube, Nabak, Urii, Wantoat, Kewieng, Rawa, Kovai); Timbe is not among them and stress is not discussed.

sources.note: No stress or accent statement anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent full text incl. spaced-scanned variants). Timbe occurs once, in the list of languages compared (p. viii area). Grammatical comparison only.
